docs.text: UI integration Add ELEA's React components to your app. Browse the component gallery . Add a button import { Button } from "@alien6-studio/elea-ui"; import "@alien6-studio/elea-ui/bundle.css"; export function DraftActions({ saveDraft }: { saveDraft: () => void }) { return <Button onClick={saveDraft}>Save draft</Button>; } This button inherits its outline from the active theme and uses its primary colour. Set variant="secondary" to give it a secondary role, or effect="ripple" to change its press gesture. Compare the same button across themes with Site theme in the header. Try Button states . Use the UI and tokens packages at the same version. The UI bundle loads both stylesheets. For a checkout, build the npm archives with npm run check -- --pack-destination artifacts . Run npm install in your app with the paths to both the UI and tokens .tgz files. Theme Browse the colour atlas to explore each theme’s photography and colour scales. The themes set the palette, typography, spacing and control shapes. Reading surfaces are white and light grey, with neutral greys in dark mode. Adjust the theme and download its CSS in Theme Studio . Load the downloaded stylesheet after the UI bundle, then set data-elea-theme="brand" on your app container. See how themes reach dialogs, sheets and toasts . Tailwind and shadcn/ui With Tailwind v4, import the bundle in your main stylesheet and declare the layer order. This keeps Preflight below the components and lets utilities override them. @layer theme, base, elea, components, utilities; @import "tailwindcss"; @import "@alien6-studio/elea-ui/bundle.css"; Add @alien6-studio/elea-tokens/theme.css to use ELEA's tokens in Tailwind utilities. See the Tailwind v3 setup and shadcn/ui integration . One sheet per component For smaller stylesheets, load the tokens once and import the styles for each component you use. @import "@alien6-studio/elea-tokens/elea.css"; @import "@alien6-studio/elea-ui/css/button.css"; See the stylesheet reference for shared sheets and form control refs. Motion Set data-elea-motion="on" on a container to enable expressive motion. It respects the visitor's reduced-motion setting. If you import individual sheets, add @alien6-studio/elea-ui/css/motion.css . Try the Expressive motion switch in the gallery . Footer The site uses ELEA's Footer component. See the Footer example for passing your own brand, link groups and signature.

docs.text: Content The viewer accepts EditorJS documents, JSON strings, HTML and plain text. Pass siteHostnames to keep links to your own site in the same tab. Provide resolveAssetUrl if your application uses a media library or protected assets. Edit a document The React editor is controlled by its host. Load the block array, pass it to the editor and save the updated blocks through your application. "use client"; import { ContentEditor, ContentProvider } from "@alien6-studio/elea-content-editor"; import "@alien6-studio/elea-content-editor/bundle.css"; <ContentProvider messages={messages} uploadImage={uploadImage} resolveAssetUrl={resolveAssetUrl} > <ContentEditor blocks={blocks} onBlocksChange={setBlocks} /> </ContentProvider>; Report what an upload is doing uploadImage receives the file, the editor context and a third argument with report and signal . Each report replaces the default uploading label; a progress between 0 and 1 adds a bar. The label is announced to assistive technology whenever it changes, so keep one label per phase and put the numbers in progress . const uploadImage: ContentEditorServices["uploadImage"] = async (file, context, { report, signal }) => { report({ label: "Uploading", progress: 0 }); const upload = await api.upload(file, { signal, onProgress: (done) => report({ label: "Uploading", progress: done }) }); report({ label: "Scanning for viruses…" }); const scan = await api.scan(upload.id, { signal }); if (!scan.clean) throw new Error("This file did not pass the virus scan."); return { id: upload.id, url: "" }; }; When the promise rejects with an Error , its message shows beside the block; the generic message stays the fallback for an empty one. signal aborts when the block is removed or its picture changes before the upload settles, so the request can be cancelled. Choose a mode mode sets how the editor presents its controls, and every mode edits the same block array. Mode What the writer gets default (Writing) Controls in the margin, a floating bar on the selection and a + menu on an empty paragraph and at the end. toolbar A fixed bar with an Insert group: one press adds the block after the focused one, or at the end when none has the focus. classic A continuous document under a formatting bar that carries the + menu. markdown A source area with line numbers. Pass mode with onModeChange to let the writer switch from the pencil menu. Edit an HTML form field The playground uses the version on main . This example requires editor and content APIs added in 0.1.3. Use mode="classic" and width="full" to fit a form column. A host can set --elea-editor-canvas-height , --elea-control-radius and --elea-control-border on the form. Its --elea-color-focus and --elea-color-selection colours carry through to the writing surface. Import the stored HTML with htmlToBlocks once when opening a record. Keep the blocks in state while editing, then call blocksToHtml when saving. Both functions come from @alien6-studio/elea-content . Set maxLength to limit the plain text and display the character counter. Try the formatted caption in the field guide . What loads when The Markdown source area, the preview and the picture cropper stay out of the editor's first load and come the first time they are asked for, each in its own chunk with a bundler that splits on dynamic imports. Until one is there the editor keeps what it shows and is aria-busy . Nothing changes in your code; to have a part ready before it is needed, ask for it: import { loadEditorParts } from "@alien6-studio/elea-content-editor"; <button onPointerEnter={() => void loadEditorParts("preview")} onClick={() => setPreview(true)}>Preview</button> A page rendered on the server with mode="markdown" or showPreview awaits loadEditorParts() before rendering, and again in the browser before hydrating. For a migration, compare the stored document before and after an edit. Keep application metadata and custom fields in your save adapter. Open the editorial workspace to edit the notebook, inspect its blocks and export the result.

docs.text: Getting started The editorial workspace shows how Elea renders and edits the glacier notebook. To build a read-only view of your own document, start with the tokens and content viewer. Install the reader Use a published release to install the reader. npm install @alien6-studio/elea-tokens @alien6-studio/elea-content-viewer Render a document import { ContentView } from "@alien6-studio/elea-content-viewer"; import "@alien6-studio/elea-content-viewer/bundle.css"; <ContentView data={storedDocument} siteHostnames={["members.example.org"]} />; Fit the host page The reader bundle loads ELEA Sans by default. Inside a page that already has its own typography, typography="inherit" takes that page's family, size, leading and colour, and sizes the headings in proportion to its text. <ContentView data={storedDocument} typography="inherit" />; The heading scale is a set of custom properties, --elea-content-heading-1 to --elea-content-heading-6 , with --elea-content-heading-family for the family. Set them on a container to keep Elea's typography and change only the scale. .article { --elea-content-heading-1: 2.5rem; --elea-content-heading-2: 2rem; } Render on a server without a DOM The default entry sanitizes stored HTML with DOMPurify, which loads jsdom on a server. The core entry is the same reader without a sanitizer of its own: it loads neither, and sanitizer becomes required. import { createSanitizer } from "@alien6-studio/elea-content"; import { ContentView } from "@alien6-studio/elea-content-viewer/core"; // `purifier` is a DOMPurify instance bound to the DOM your server already has const sanitizer = createSanitizer(purifier, { links: { siteHostnames: ["members.example.org"] } }); <ContentView data={storedDocument} sanitizer={sanitizer} />; What the sanitizer returns is written to the page as HTML: it is the only thing between stored content and your readers. For an unpublished checkout, see the repository instructions for building and qualifying the npm archives.

docs.text: Observe Alien6 Observe is a TypeScript SDK that records what happens to the controls you register: an activation, a focus change, an exposure, a state transition or the outcome of a task. It has no dependency and does not require ELEA. It keeps the records in memory and sends nothing. npm install @alien6-studio/observe The package is released with the ELEA packages, under the same version, from 0.1.5. Three things to declare You declare What it does A catalog Lists every target you allow, with its context and its event kinds. An event that matches no entry is rejected. A grant Starts collection for one purpose and a set of event kinds. Until the host gives one, nothing is recorded. Bindings Attach a registered target to a DOM element, for the events a browser can establish. A target names a control by its function, not by its label or position: a surface , a component , a slot such as document.save , a role , and the current state and variant or null . The context carries the theme, appearance, density and experiment arm, each null when unknown. Every code is 1 to 64 characters among lowercase letters, digits, . , _ and - . Record a save This example counts the clicks on a save button and records whether the save succeeded. The browser establishes the click. The application reports the outcome, because only it knows the document was stored. import { createLocalObserve, type ObserveCatalogV1, type ObserveContextV1, type ObserveTargetV1, } from "@alien6-studio/observe"; import { createBrowserCollector } from "@alien6-studio/observe/browser"; const save = { surface: "editor", component: "button", slot: "document.save", role: "button", state: "ready", variant: null, } satisfies ObserveTargetV1; const context = { theme: null, appearance: null, density: null, experiment: null } satisfies ObserveContextV1; const catalog = { revision: "editor-1", entries: [{ target: save, context, kinds: ["interaction.activated", "task.outcome"], tasks: ["document.save"], }], } satisfies ObserveCatalogV1; const observe = createLocalObserve({ purpose: "local-demo", catalog, collectors: [ createBrowserCollector([{ element: button, target: () => save, activation: true }], () => context), ], }); // Nothing is recorded before the grant. observe.setGrant({ purpose: "local-demo", destination: "memory", kinds: ["interaction.activated", "task.outcome"], }); // Once the document is stored: observe.record({ schemaVersion: 1, kind: "task.outcome", target: save, context, detail: { source: "application-task", task: "document.save", outcome: "succeeded", duration: "under-1s" }, }); observe.snapshot(); // the records, oldest first observe.setGrant(null); // stops collection and clears the records record returns false when it refuses an event. snapshot returns frozen records, each with an index , an elapsedMs rounded to 10 ms and the event . The buffer holds 128 records by default, 1,024 at most, and drops the oldest first. subscribe calls a listener after each change, to refresh a display. dispose ends the instance. The five events Event Reported by It establishes interaction.activated A binding with activation , or record for an application command The target was activated. The modality stays unknown unless the source proves it. focus.changed A binding with focus DOM focus entered or left the element. exposure.qualified A binding with exposure and a catalog rule The element kept a minimum share of its area in the viewport of a visible document for a minimum time. It does not establish that anyone looked at it. state.transitioned record The target moved from a state listed in fromStates to its current state . task.outcome record A task listed in tasks succeeded, failed or was cancelled, with a duration band or null . A binding only reports trusted browser events on a connected element, and ignores a control that is disabled or inert. Use one activation source per action: the click binding or the application command, not both. What it leaves to you Consent and purpose. The host decides when to grant and when to revoke. Replacing or revoking a grant detaches the listeners and discards the records. Delivery. The SDK stores, transfers and exports nothing, and refuses a grant whose destination is export . Content. The event has no field for a label, a form value, a URL, a coordinate or an identifier of a person, a device or a session. Keep them out of the codes you register. Untrusted input. createEventValidator(catalog) checks a value against the catalog and returns a frozen event or null . The Interaction Observatory explains what each event can support as a claim, and its laboratory runs this SDK on a save. To display records, the UI package provides measurement displays .

docs.text: Research Studies of form, composition and interaction. Each connects a worked construction to published evidence and identifies the decisions that remain in the designer’s hands. Geometry of interfaces Corners, curvature, nested contours and optical corrections: one radius hides four decisions, and this study measures each of them. Read the study , with its sources and computed figures. Open the atlas : six plates, each with the numbers behind its drawing. Open the laboratory : the same functions applied to working components. A 40-rem frame Archive at 46 rem The note sits beside the passage. The comparison is paired and the index fits 3 entries in its first row. A 46-rem frame The upper band shows the record and its outlined note, the middle band a comparison, and the lower band an index of three recordings. The frames use the same horizontal scale. The three views above share six columns and the same margins. The useful difference lies in what each piece of content needs from those columns. A passage needs a sustained line of type. A note needs an edge near the passage it describes. The collection needs room for a succession of names. The worked series derives the different widths at which each arrangement becomes possible. A grid supplies positions to return to across a composition. Its geometry can be specified exactly. Whether it helps a reader compare two entries requires observation. Which entry gets the larger field, and where the designer leaves space around it, are artistic decisions. Establish the field Draw the final frame, then mark the space the composition can occupy. Measure that panel. A marginal note outside the text block still needs to fit inside the frame. If the frame width is W and its two side margins are L and R , the available width is A = W − L − R . Moving four units from the left margin to the right preserves the measure of every column but moves every leading edge four units to the left. The text rectangle measures 2W/3 × 2H/3 , so it keeps the page's aspect ratio and occupies four ninths of its area. Mirror the horizontal margins on the facing page. Across an open, flat spread the two inner margins add up to one outer margin. The deeper margin sits below the text on both pages. Facing pages divided into ninths The composition is mirrored at the fold. The outside margin of each page is twice its inside margin. The lower margin is twice the upper margin. A facing-page construction in ninths. Each text field keeps its page’s proportions. At the fold, the two inner margins together equal one outer margin. On a 180 × 270 mm page the text block is 120 × 180 mm. Increase the page width to 210 mm and this construction gives the text 140 mm. If the type and line breaks of the original edition are worth keeping, retain the 120 mm measure and distribute the extra 30 mm in the margins. These are distinct briefs. One preserves proportions, the other preserves the setting of the text. Construct the columns For N equal columns and a uniform gutter G , there are N − 1 gutters. Subtract their total width before dividing the available field. With one column the entire available width belongs to it. Each column has width C = (A − (N − 1)G) / N . A block spanning k consecutive columns has width S(k) = kC + (k − 1)G . Numbering from one, column j starts at x(j) = L + (j − 1)(C + G) in a left-to-right field. The construction needs positive column width, an integer N ≥ 1 and a span from one through N . A block spanning two columns takes the gutter inside its footprint. A separate neighbouring block leaves the gutter between them open. The last column must end at W − R . 3 plus 3 columns Six tracks of 29 units, with two occupied spans of 99 and 99 separated by one six-unit gutter. 99 99 Three + three 2 plus 4 columns Six tracks of 29 units, with two occupied spans of 64 and 134 separated by one six-unit gutter. 64 134 Two + four Both frames measure 240 × 160 units. Six 29-unit columns occupy the same positions in each. Changing the span assignment moves the division while preserving the margins and the separating gutter. Take a 240-unit frame with 18 units on either side. The live field is 204 units wide. Six columns with five 6-unit gutters leave 174 units for type and artwork, or 29 per column. Two blocks spanning three columns each are 99 units wide. Giving one block two columns and the other four yields widths of 64 and 134, with the same 6-unit gutter. A 2:4 division in column count therefore produces a slightly wider than 2:1 ratio between the actual blocks. The gutter has a cost. Double it from 6 to 12 while keeping the frame, margins and six columns. Each column shrinks from 29 to 24. The note spanning two columns loses four units of measure (64 to 60), while the passage spanning four loses only two (134 to 132). Set a full line on each side of the gap and check whether the two passages remain distinct and both still read well. A six-column grid can carry halves, thirds and sixths without moving its guides. A four-column grid can carry quarters and halves. Choose between them by listing the arrangements a series actually needs. An essay and an occasional pair of examples may need only two columns. Adding guides that no element uses introduces choices without adding a usable alignment. Give the spans a purpose For sustained reading , give the text a continuous measure. A heading may use the same leading edge and span a greater width. Keep its line endings independent of the body so that a long title can wrap without widening every paragraph. For explanation beside a reference , let the narrower region contain the shorter material, such as dates, notes or an index. Give their common edge a specific job. Follow a note across that edge to its corresponding passage. If the relationship repeatedly crosses a page turn, the rail needs a local reference or a different position. An asymmetric grid can be made with unequal spans on equal columns, as the column plate shows. For a collection , repeat a set of fields for items of equal rank. An exceptional item can span two fields, but decide what warrants that emphasis and where the next ordinary item resumes. Empty modules can also carry meaning. They make different pairs out of the same words. Departures with space before the platform The three services have the same times, destinations and platforms. One column is empty before the platform. One column is empty after the time. Departures 08:10 North Pier Platform 2 08:40 Dry Dock Platform 1 09:20 Tide Mill Platform 3 Destination beside platform Read across the 08:40 service. Dry Dock moves by one column. The times and platforms stay in place, and all three fields retain their width. In the first setting, time and destination share a 6-unit gutter. Before the platform come a gutter, an empty 29-unit column and another gutter, 41 units in all. Move the empty column to the other side of the destination and the gaps exchange places. The outside edges, occupied area and number of alignments cannot tell the two settings apart. Which space to leave open depends on which two pieces someone needs to read together. These gaps are measured between fields. A short name such as Dry Dock leaves more space between its last letter and the next field. Leyssen and colleagues asked people to compose or choose pictures of familiar objects. Participants preferred related objects closer together than unrelated ones. A preference for centring emerged most clearly when the distance within the pair was fixed. Their subject was pictorial preference. For the board this suggests a testable question. Would someone starting from a departure time find its destination faster in the first setting? Would someone starting from a destination find its platform faster in the second? Each question has a different starting point and a measurable answer. Leyssen et al., Aesthetic Preference for Spatial Composition in Multi-Object Pictures (2012) . A module is the field at the intersection of a column and a row. A baseline grid supplies the lines on which type can sit. Its step can be much finer than a module. Module rows Two baseline sequences Starting on the same ruling, lines set 16 units apart and 24 units apart meet again after 48 and 96 units. 16- and 24-unit leading The first ruling lies 16 units below the top of the frame. An 8-unit step locates both the modules and the ideal text baselines. The two sequences on the right coincide every 48 units. In the module plate the first horizontal guide sits at 16 and successive guides are 8 units apart. A module three steps deep is 24 units high. Leave one step between modules and the row starts are 16, 48, 80 and 112. An item spanning two rows occupies 24 + 8 + 24 = 56 units. The final row ends at 136 in the 160-unit frame, leaving 24 units below. The lower margin is a choice visible in the construction. To align type across columns, set the first actual baseline and the advance to the next one. In the plate both columns start at 16. With advances of 16 on the left and 24 on the right, the two sequences meet again at 64 and 112. The repeat interval is 48, the least common multiple of the two advances. Giving two text boxes the same top edge and line height alone cannot guarantee the same first baseline for different fonts. Check where the letters sit inside the rendered line boxes. A printed catalogue can allocate a second row to a long entry or continue it on the next page. On screen a description may grow after the reader opens it or enlarges the type. Let the row grow and resume the rhythm below it. A fixed module that clips a description preserves the arithmetic at the cost of the content. An alternative construction derives the vertical unit from the chosen leading and divides the field afterwards. IBM Design Language, baseline unit . Find where the grid stops fitting Record a minimum usable width for each role after setting representative material. Suppose a note requires 60 units and the main passage 100. These are design constraints for this example. In the six-column construction the proposed note spans two columns, so its width is 2C + 6 . The note fits when C ≥ 27 . The passage spans four columns and needs 4C + 18 ≥ 100 , which gives C ≥ 20.5 . The note therefore sets the limit. With the original margins and gutters, the smallest frame for this allocation is 18 + 6 × 27 + 5 × 6 + 18 = 228 units. There the two blocks measure 60 and 126. At 222 units they measure 58 and 122. The main passage still fits and the note has already failed. A narrower setting can bring the note into the text flow and give both elements a single column. A different gutter or span would give a different threshold. Choose the narrow reading order before moving the regions. Keep a note with the passage it explains, a heading with the section it introduces, and a label with its value. For interactive work, follow the focus sequence as well as reading the words. For ordinary vertically scrolling text, also check reflow at 320 CSS pixels. WCAG 2.2, Meaningful Sequence · Focus Order · Reflow . One ruling for a family of views Consider a small sound archive. Its record view sets a passage beside a field note. Its comparison gives two recordings equal space. Its index repeats an entry three times across the field. Begin with the divisions these tasks require. Halves and thirds can both end on the lines of six equal columns. Six is the smallest count divisible by both two and three. If quarters must also align across views, the smallest count becomes twelve. A quarter used only inside a single entry can be a local division. The margins and gutters matter as much as the count. In the 240-unit construction above, a four-column field is 134 units wide. Divide it in two with the original 6-unit gutter and each half is 64 units. The halves recover the edges of the underlying two-column spans. With a local gutter of 2 units, the halves become 66 units. The centre of the gutter stays at 67, but each of its edges moves by 2. Running the equation in reverse gives the frame at which a span first reaches a chosen measure m . The result is W = L + R − G + (N/k)(m + G) . Each occupied region sets its own limit. The widest of the required lower bounds tells us when the whole row fits. A maximum reading measure can also set an upper bound. Two recordings fit side by side. A two-column note gets only 11⅓ rem. It belongs below the passage at this width. The index fits two entries on its first row and carries the third to the next. A single switch for all three views would give up a viable comparison or squeeze the note. The interface can keep the same outer edges through all three changes. The comparison still fits. The note moves below the record and the third index entry starts a new row. Closing the rail restores all three arrangements. The width that matters here can be measured between the sides of the working pane. For this edition, the whole frame stops growing at 54 rem . At that width the four-column passage reaches its chosen maximum of 33 rem. Extra space falls equally outside the edition and the three views keep their common edges. Another edition could let the collection grow wider and cap only the text inside the reading view. Its index would gain space at the cost of that edge matching across views. When a proportion has no solution Suppose the note must now accommodate an 18-rem transcription. On the four-plus-two division the note reaches that measure at 60 rem , while the passage reaches its ceiling at 54 rem . No frame width meets both conditions. Doubling the ruling to twelve and assigning eight columns to the passage and four to the note leaves their widths exactly as before. Changing the allocation does help. On two equal fields, a frame of 51 rem gives each side 23 rem. Both pieces fit, the first line of the passage starts on its usual edge, and the note moves inward by one column. Below 51 rem the note can follow its passage in reading order. Try the three views at the same width . The width of an actual label What does the proposed measure buy in type? The plates use abstract units and ideal edges. A physical fold has thickness, and a rasterised line may occupy fractional pixels. Verify the final edge on the intended medium. Changing a display width while holding text size constant is a new layout condition. Uniformly scaling down a drawing preserves only its geometry. Reading. Readers nevertheless rated the 55-character lines easiest. A fastest line, a preferred line and a line that improves comprehension can be three different claims. Their items stayed in place. Widening a gutter moves items as well as separating them. It cannot tell an editor which passage deserves the emphasis. What a layout system can carry from one view to the next Give a recurring edge a name in the composition. In the archive, the record title, the first listening position and the first collection entry start on the same line. The far edge of the passage is free to change. On the board, the open column separates one pair of fields so that the other pair sits together. A narrow gutter can make the note look like a continuation of the passage. A wide one can draw it towards the next passage. Which separation helps the reader match the note to the right text? One comparison would keep the page size, type and line lengths fixed. The extra width for the gutter would come equally from the two outer margins. Readers would match notes to passages, encountering each passage only once. Reversing the order of the layouts and exchanging the passages between them would help distinguish the effect of the layout from the difficulty of a particular text. Correct matches would tell us about reading. A separate preference judgement would tell us which page readers liked. Readers might prefer the more open page and make the same number of correct matches in both. The question remains open for these layouts. The atlas follows one programme through three compositions. In the module plate the first horizontal guide sits at 16 and successive guides are 8 units apart. A module three steps deep is 24 units high. Leave one step between modules and the row starts are 16, 48, 80 and 112. An item spanning two rows occupies 24 + 8 + 24 = 56 units. The final row ends at 136 in the 160-unit frame, leaving 24 units below. The lower margin is a choice visible in the construction. To align type across columns, set the first actual baseline and the advance to the next one. In the plate both columns start at 16. With advances of 16 on the left and 24 on the right, the two sequences meet again at 64 and 112. The repeat interval is 48, the least common multiple of the two advances. docs.title: Set modules and baselines

docs.text: Record a minimum usable width for each role after setting representative material. Suppose a note requires 60 units and the main passage 100. These are design constraints for this example. In the six-column construction the proposed note spans two columns, so its width is 2C + 6 . The note fits when C ≥ 27 . The passage spans four columns and needs 4C + 18 ≥ 100 , which gives C ≥ 20.5 . The note therefore sets the limit. With the original margins and gutters, the smallest frame for this allocation is 18 + 6 × 27 + 5 × 6 + 18 = 228 units. There the two blocks measure 60 and 126. At 222 units they measure 58 and 122. The main passage still fits and the note has already failed. A narrower setting can bring the note into the text flow and give both elements a single column. A different gutter or span would give a different threshold. Choose the narrow reading order before moving the regions. Keep a note with the passage it explains, a heading with the section it introduces, and a label with its value. For interactive work, follow the focus sequence as well as reading the words. For ordinary vertically scrolling text, also check reflow at 320 CSS pixels. WCAG 2.2, Meaningful Sequence · Focus Order · Reflow .
docs.title: Find where the grid stops fitting

docs.text: Consider a small sound archive. Its record view sets a passage beside a field note. Its comparison gives two recordings equal space. Its index repeats an entry three times across the field. Begin with the divisions these tasks require. Halves and thirds can both end on the lines of six equal columns. Six is the smallest count divisible by both two and three. If quarters must also align across views, the smallest count becomes twelve. A quarter used only inside a single entry can be a local division. The margins and gutters matter as much as the count. In the 240-unit construction above, a four-column field is 134 units wide. Divide it in two with the original 6-unit gutter and each half is 64 units. The halves recover the edges of the underlying two-column spans. With a local gutter of 2 units, the halves become 66 units. The centre of the gutter stays at 67, but each of its edges moves by 2. For a caption that must line up with the next row, the distinction is visible at the first letter. Two working systems show different reasons to keep an edge across a series. In the US National Park Service's Unigrid, the folds define 4 × 8¼ inch panels. A brochure can be one or two panels wide and up to six panels long. The folded format and the size of a press sheet constrain the family while each park can give its map a different extent. National Park Service, A Brief History of the Unigrid . In the GOV.UK Design System, the main text can keep its two-thirds measure both on pages with secondary material and on pages where the last third is empty. Here the repeated decision concerns the reading column. The space at its side is available to the composition without obliging an editor to fill it. GOV.UK Design System, Layout .
docs.title: One ruling for a family of views

docs.text: For the archive, take a margin of 2 rem on each side and a gutter of 1 rem. One rem is the size of the root type on screen. Let the passage occupy four columns and the field note two. The editor gives the passage a measure between 23 and 33 rem and reserves at least 12 rem for the note. These are settings for this specimen. A different face, language or task may call for other measures. At frame width W , the width of a span is S(k) = (k/N)(W − L − R + G) − G . Running the equation in reverse gives the frame at which a span first reaches a chosen measure m . The result is W = L + R − G + (N/k)(m + G) . Each occupied region sets its own limit. The widest of the required lower bounds tells us when the whole row fits. A maximum reading measure can also set an upper bound. Three views on the same six columns View Measure chosen for this setting Where the arrangement fits Record and field note Passage 23–33 rem, note at least 12 rem Four plus two columns from 42 to 54 rem Comparison Each recording at least 16 rem Two equal fields from 37 rem Index Each entry at least 13 rem Two across from 31 rem, three from 45 rem At 40 rem , half the field is 17.5 rem once the intervening gutter is allowed for. Two recordings fit side by side. A two-column note gets only 11⅓ rem. It belongs below the passage at this width. The index fits two entries on its first row and carries the third to the next. A single switch for all three views would give up a viable comparison or squeeze the note. The interface can keep the same outer edges through all three changes. An interface often changes width without the window moving at all. Take a 56-rem workspace. Opening a 14-rem navigation rail with a 1-rem gap leaves 41 rem for the working view. The comparison still fits. The note moves below the record and the third index entry starts a new row. Closing the rail restores all three arrangements. The width that matters here can be measured between the sides of the working pane. For this edition, the whole frame stops growing at 54 rem . At that width the four-column passage reaches its chosen maximum of 33 rem. Extra space falls equally outside the edition and the three views keep their common edges. Another edition could let the collection grow wider and cap only the text inside the reading view. Its index would gain space at the cost of that edge matching across views.
docs.title: Different views change at different widths

docs.text: Suppose the note must now accommodate an 18-rem transcription. On the four-plus-two division the note reaches that measure at 60 rem , while the passage reaches its ceiling at 54 rem . No frame width meets both conditions. Doubling the ruling to twelve and assigning eight columns to the passage and four to the note leaves their widths exactly as before. Changing the allocation does help. On two equal fields, a frame of 51 rem gives each side 23 rem. Both pieces fit, the first line of the passage starts on its usual edge, and the note moves inward by one column. Below 51 rem the note can follow its passage in reading order. Try the three views at the same width .
docs.title: When a proportion has no solution

docs.text: What does the proposed measure buy in type? Take the short label East landing microphone . A two-column slot in the 40-rem frame is 11⅓ rem wide, or about 181.3 pixels with the root type set to 16 pixels. The two settings below use that exact measure, a 1-rem type size, medium weight and zero added letterspacing. Only the typeface changes. Instrument Sans East landing microphone Roboto East landing microphone The outlines mark the slot the note would receive if the 40-rem record kept its two regions side by side. Instrument Sans wraps after “landing”. Roboto fits on one line. At that size the unbroken label measured 185.1 pixels in Instrument Sans and 177.2 in Roboto in our Chromium setting. The wider label East landing and harbour wall microphones measured 318.9 and 308.4 pixels. Neither fits on one line in the proposed 18 rem (288 pixels). If a line break is acceptable, the note can keep that measure. Keeping the label on one line changes the brief. Within a two-column span on this ruling, each extra unit of required label width costs three units of frame width. A different string or a different font file needs its own measurement. Reading speed would require a reader study.
docs.title: The width of an actual label

docs.text: Construction. Track widths, alignment coordinates, spans and the positions of horizontal guides can all be calculated. The plates use abstract units and ideal edges. A physical fold has thickness, and a rasterised line may occupy fractional pixels. Verify the final edge on the intended medium. Changing a display width while holding text size constant is a new layout condition. Uniformly scaling down a drawing preserves only its geometry. Reading. Dyson and Kipping compared line lengths in screen reading. Their 100-character lines were read faster than 25-character lines, with no observed difference in comprehension. Readers nevertheless rated the 55-character lines easiest. A fastest line, a preferred line and a line that improves comprehension can be three different claims. The results apply to the texts, type and screen conditions studied. The Effects of Line Length and Method of Movement on Patterns of Reading from Screen (1998) . Grouping. Brumby and Zhuang asked 36 people to find named words in menus. When the words were randomly arranged, adding boxes around groups increased mean correct search time from 3.95 to 4.51 seconds. Their items stayed in place. Widening a gutter moves items as well as separating them. The result gives a reason to check the meaning of a group before drawing its boundaries and leaves the effective gutter for any new layout open. Visual Grouping in Menu Interfaces (2015) . Art direction. The 3+3 and 2+4 arrangements both close exactly at the outer margins. Use equal spans when the items deserve equivalent treatment, or deliberately give one more space when it introduces the other. Arithmetic can reveal an unintended offset. It cannot tell an editor which passage deserves the emphasis.
docs.title: What measurements can establish

docs.text: Give a recurring edge a name in the composition. In the archive, the record title, the first listening position and the first collection entry start on the same line. The far edge of the passage is free to change. A designer can now draw a fourth view and say exactly which edge it inherits. A locally divided field can meet the parent lines again when it inherits their gutter as well as their extent. Specify the relationship each arrangement serves. Two equal spans give the recordings equivalent treatment. The unequal record gives the passage more room and keeps its note nearby. On the board, the open column separates one pair of fields so that the other pair sits together. Translating the words or reversing the reading direction can preserve those relationships even as the physical positions change. Write a condition for leaving the arrangement. Set representative words in the intended face, work back from each required measure, and keep the intersection of the resulting ranges. If the intersection is empty, choose a different division or put the items in reading order on separate rows. This is where a family can share a drawing rule and still have different transitions. Six columns, 2-rem margins and a 54-rem ceiling describe one edition of the archive. The reasoning also works for another edition with different type and different dimensions.
docs.title: What a layout system can carry from one view to the next

docs.text: In the six-column example, arithmetic tells us the smallest width at which the note fits. It leaves another question open. A narrow gutter can make the note look like a continuation of the passage. A wide one can draw it towards the next passage. Which separation helps the reader match the note to the right text? One comparison would keep the page size, type and line lengths fixed. The extra width for the gutter would come equally from the two outer margins. Readers would match notes to passages, encountering each passage only once. Reversing the order of the layouts and exchanging the passages between them would help distinguish the effect of the layout from the difficulty of a particular text. Correct matches would tell us about reading. A separate preference judgement would tell us which page readers liked. Readers might prefer the more open page and make the same number of correct matches in both. The question remains open for these layouts. The atlas follows one programme through three compositions. In the laboratory, open the collection navigation while keeping the window still, then compare which parts of the archive change. Atlas · Laboratory .
docs.title: How far from a passage should its note sit?

docs.text: Geometry of interfaces A rounded rectangle is specified by one number, yet its corner involves four independent decisions: how deep the corner is cut, how far along the edge the curve begins, how the curvature is distributed, and how an inner contour follows an outer one. This study separates those decisions, measures them, and sorts each statement into one of three kinds: geometry that can be proved, perception that has to be tested, and artistic choice. Lengths are given in units of r , the radius of the circular corner taken as reference. The atlas draws the same constructions as plates, and the laboratory applies them to working components. A corner is a transition A circular corner joins two straight edges with a quarter circle. Tangents agree at the joins, so the contour has no kink: it is continuous in direction, which geometers call G1. Its curvature is not continuous. It is zero on the edge and 1/r on the arc, with a step between them. A contour whose curvature also varies without a step is called G2. Three constructions remove the step. A superellipse flattens the curve near the joins. An Euler spiral, whose curvature grows in proportion to the distance travelled, can lead into a shorter circular arc and out of it again; Raph Levien's thesis is the reference treatment of that curve. A single cubic Bézier with both handles placed on the vertex also starts and ends with zero curvature, and is the simplest of the three to write. These curves cannot be compared at equal radius, because the radius does not mean the same thing for each of them. They are compared here at equal cut : every curve passes through the same point of the diagonal, 0.41 r from the vertex. Four corner curves drawn through the same point on the diagonal 1.00 Circular arc 1.84 Superellipse, exponent 4 1.30 Spiral, arc, spiral 2.34 Cubic, handles on the vertex Shared cut, 0.41 r r Four corners that remove the same depth from the vertex. The figures on the top edge give the distance, in radii of the circular arc, at which each curve leaves the edge. Curvature along the contour for the four corners 0.5 1.0 1.5 -2 -1 0 1 2 Distance along the contour from the middle of the corner, in r Curvature × r Curvature of the four corners of the previous figure. The circular arc jumps from zero to 1/r. The three others start from zero, and pay for it with a higher peak and a longer transition. Corner, at equal cut Length taken on the edge Curvature at the join Peak curvature Largest distance to the circular corner Circular arc 1.00 r step to 1/r 1.00 / r 0 Spiral, arc, spiral 1.30 r 0 1.09 / r 0.012 r Superellipse, exponent 4 1.84 r 0 1.37 / r 0.028 r Cubic, handles on the vertex 2.34 r 0 1.61 / r 0.044 r Two consequences follow, and both are arithmetic. Continuity is paid for in length and in sharpness. A corner that starts from zero curvature must turn the same quarter turn, so it turns harder in the middle and begins earlier on the edge. The superellipse takes 84% more of the edge than the arc it replaces. On a control whose height is less than 3.7 r , two such corners no longer fit on the short side. At control sizes the difference is below a pixel. Once the cut is matched, the superellipse never departs from the circular corner by more than 0.028 r : 0.23 CSS pixel for an 8 px corner, 0.45 for 16 px, 0.91 for 32 px. The spiral blend stays within 0.19 px at 16 px. On a button or a field, a continuous corner changes a few antialiased pixels. On a card, a sheet or a photograph it changes a visible band. Whether observers see that difference, and from which size, is not established by any source consulted for this study. It is a hypothesis to test, not a result. One number for the curve A superellipse corner satisfies |x/a|ⁿ + |y/b|ⁿ = 1 . The exponent n sets the distribution of curvature: 2 gives the ellipse, larger values push the curve towards the vertex, 1 gives a straight bevel. CSS Borders and Box Decorations Level 4, a W3C working draft, exposes this as corner-shape: superellipse(K) , where the exponent is 2ᴷ . That reading is the one consistent with the keywords the draft defines: bevel is superellipse(0) , round is superellipse(1) , squircle is superellipse(2) , and negative values mirror the curve into scoop and notch . The value interpolates, so a corner can animate from one shape to another. Superellipse corners from notch to square K = −∞ notch K = −1 scoop K = 0 bevel K = 0.5 K = 1 round K = 2 squircle K = ∞ square One number per corner. CSS superellipse(K) draws a quarter superellipse of exponent 2 K inside the box set by border-radius . The property keeps border-radius as the box in which the corner is drawn. A squircle with the radius of a round corner is therefore cut 0.22 r deep where the round one is cut 0.41 r : it reads as a smaller radius. Much of what is attributed to the smoothness of an uncompensated squircle is a change of size. The two can be separated. A corner of curve K keeps the cut of a round corner of radius r when its radius is multiplied by (1 − 2^(−1/2)) / (1 − 2^(−1/2ᴷ)) which gives 1.35 for K = 1.5 , 1.84 for K = 2 and 2.54 for K = 2.5 . The factor is a pure function of K and can be written in CSS with pow() . Matching the removed area instead of the cut gives 1.72 for K = 2 ; which of the two looks equal is a question for an experiment. round , radius 1.25rem superellipse(2) , same radius superellipse(2) , radius × 1.84 Live rendering. This browser does not implement corner-shape : the three boxes are drawn with the same circular corners, which is the intended fallback. Where the property is supported, the third box keeps the depth of the first and changes only the distribution of curvature. corner-shape shipped in Chrome and Edge 139. Firefox and Safari do not implement it at the time of writing, and MDN lists it as limited availability. Borders, outlines, shadows and overflow clipping follow the shaped contour, which clip-path and masks cannot offer: they cut the border, the shadow and the focus ring away with the rest. Nested contours For an inset d smaller than a circular corner's radius R , a concentric arc of radius R − d gives a constant gap. A parallel contour can also keep a constant gap inside a superellipse. Construct it by moving a distance d along the inward normal at each point, as shown in the atlas . The gap between an outer and an inner corner in three constructions d 1.41 d Equal radii d 1.00 d Radius minus inset d 1.19 d Superellipse, scaled The gap between two nested contours, measured on the edge and on the diagonal. Subtracting the inset from the radius keeps the gap constant for circular arcs. Equal circular radii leave a diagonal gap of √2 d in the example, 41% wider than on the edges. Radius minus inset keeps the gap constant for circular corners. When the inset reaches the radius, the inner corner is square. Superellipses do not nest by subtraction. An inner squircle of radius R − d leaves a diagonal gap 19% wider than d at d = R/4 and 14% wider at d = R/2 . The exact inner contour is not a superellipse; the draft specification says as much, and browsers compute it for borders themselves. Elliptical corners behave the same way. For a corner of 1.5rem / 0.625rem , subtracting an inset of 0.3125rem from both radii leaves a gap that narrows by 13% along the curve. Optical corrections Geometry gives candidates; it does not say which one looks right. Equal width, equal area and centroid constructions Square, side 18 Circle of the same width, 18 Keyline circle, 20 Circle of the same area, 20.31 Centred on its box Centred on its centroid Left: three candidate sizes for a circle meant to weigh as much as a square. Right: a triangle centred on its bounding box and on its centroid, one sixth of its height apart. A circle inscribed in a square covers 79% of its area and looks smaller. The circle of equal area has a diameter of 2/√π , or 1.128 times the side. The keylines of Material's system icons use a 20 dp circle with an 18 dp square, a ratio of 1.111, close to equal area and rounded to the grid. A triangle centred on its bounding box sits one sixth of its height away from its centroid, which is why play glyphs are shifted towards their point. Equal area and centroid alignment are demonstrable constructions. That they match perceived size and perceived centre is a working rule of practitioners, to be checked for each glyph. What the references do Apple offers two corner curves on a layer, circular and continuous, and SwiftUI adds concentric shapes whose radius is the container's radius minus the distance between the corners, with an optional minimum. The continuous curve is not published as a formula. Figma's analysis of the iOS icon found that no superellipse reproduces it and that its curvature profile is assembled from several Bézier segments; Figma's own corner smoothing joins a circular arc to the edges with Bézier transitions. Nesting is solved in the layout system, where the distance is known. Material Design treats shape as a polygon with rounded vertices that can morph into another polygon, through the androidx.graphics.shapes library. The contribution is motion between shapes; its corners remain circular arcs with an optional smoothing parameter. Fluent 2 publishes a short radius scale, from 2 px to 12 px and the circle, and ties the step to the size of the element. It does not state a rule for nested corners. Carbon builds on a 2x grid and keeps rectangular geometry; its icon guidelines specify a 2 px corner. No corner-radius token was found in its documentation. Three observations hold across them. Curvature continuity is adopted where surfaces are large and hardware is curved, and ignored for small controls, which agrees with the pixel arithmetic above. Nesting needs the distance between the contours, so it belongs to layout and not to a static token. None of these systems publishes perceptual evidence for its corner curve. On perception, the literature supports less than is often claimed. Bar and Neta reported a preference for curved over sharp-cornered objects. Bertamini and colleagues found that the effect is an attraction to curvature and not an avoidance of angles. Both concern object contours, not the choice between two rounded corners of different continuity. Three kinds of statement Demonstrable To test with observers Artistic decision A circular corner has a curvature step; superellipses above exponent 2, spiral blends and vertex cubics do not. From which corner size the step is noticed, and whether it affects preference. Whether a brand's contours are tense, soft or cut. At equal cut, a continuous corner is longer on the edge and sharper at its apex. Whether equal cut or equal area makes two corners look the same size. Asymmetry: which corners differ, and what the difference stands for. Subtracting the inset gives a constant gap between circular arcs. A normal offset gives a parallel contour for other curves. The gap variation that observers tolerate before nesting looks wrong. The minimum radius below which an inner corner becomes square. Equal-area and centroid constructions for glyphs. Their agreement with perceived size and centre. The proportions of surfaces and the rhythm of radii across a scale. Rules for a design system Five rules follow from the sections above. Each one is decided by measuring the contours a system draws: it holds or it is broken, on every contour, and a contour it does not constrain cannot break it. A curve keeps the cut of the radius scale. A radius fixes how deep a corner is cut; the distribution of curvature is a second parameter. A contour drawn with a curve other than the arc has its radius multiplied by the factor given above, so that it cuts as deep as a step of the scale. A continuous curve is used where it can be seen. At equal cut, a continuous corner that stays within one device pixel of the circular one is drawn as an arc: the curve changes nothing there and takes more of the edge. Inlaid arcs share a centre. For an inner circular corner that sits the same distance from both edges and inside the outer arc, use max(minimum, outer radius − inset) . With elliptical corners, subtracting the inset on each axis aligns the centres and the gap varies. A container can pad its content clear of its corner curves. The minimum radius is an artistic decision. A rounded contour is drawn by its border, not by a clip. A contour drawn with corner-shape carries the border, the shadow and the focus outline with it, and falls back to an arc where the property is missing. A clip path or a mask removes all three. Two steps of a scale are a pixel apart, or they are one step. A scale offers a choice, and a choice no screen can draw is not one. Steps derived from a shape by a ratio collapse when the shape is fine: half and three quarters of a 3 px radius are 0.75 px apart. A system that derives its steps measures them on the contours they are meant for, and falls back to steps that can be told apart. Open questions Two statements of this study are not rules, because no measurement of a contour decides them. Optical corrections. Equal area and centroid alignment are sound starting constructions for a glyph. Whether they look right is a matter of perception, untested here. The default curve. A paired comparison of circular and continuous corners at equal cut, across sizes and pixel densities, would turn the central hypothesis of this page into a result. Until one exists, the circular arc is the default that can be defended. Method and limits Curves are sampled as polylines of 1,600 segments per corner; curvature is the inverse radius of the circle through three consecutive samples. The spiral blend spends half of its turn in the two spirals. Gaps are the distance from each sample of the inner contour to the nearest point of the outer one. The study measures contours, not rendered pixels: antialiasing, stroke alignment and subpixel layout are outside its scope. Statements about Apple's continuous corner rely on Apple's API documentation and on Figma's published analysis, not on a specification. No experiment with observers has been run. docs.text: Apple offers two corner curves on a layer, circular and continuous, and SwiftUI adds concentric shapes whose radius is the container's radius minus the distance between the corners, with an optional minimum. Figma's analysis of the iOS icon found that no superellipse reproduces it and that its curvature profile is assembled from several Bézier segments; Figma's own corner smoothing joins a circular arc to the edges with Bézier transitions. Nesting is solved in the layout system, where the distance is known. Material Design treats shape as a polygon with rounded vertices that can morph into another polygon, through the androidx.graphics.shapes library. docs.text: Five rules follow from the sections above. Each one is decided by measuring the contours a system draws: it holds or it is broken, on every contour, and a contour it does not constrain cannot break it. A curve keeps the cut of the radius scale. A radius fixes how deep a corner is cut; the distribution of curvature is a second parameter. A contour drawn with a curve other than the arc has its radius multiplied by the factor given above, so that it cuts as deep as a step of the scale. A continuous curve is used where it can be seen. At equal cut, a continuous corner that stays within one device pixel of the circular one is drawn as an arc: the curve changes nothing there and takes more of the edge. Inlaid arcs share a centre. For an inner circular corner that sits the same distance from both edges and inside the outer arc, use max(minimum, outer radius − inset) . With elliptical corners, subtracting the inset on each axis aligns the centres and the gap varies. A container can pad its content clear of its corner curves. The minimum radius is an artistic decision. A rounded contour is drawn by its border, not by a clip. A contour drawn with corner-shape carries the border, the shadow and the focus outline with it, and falls back to an arc where the property is missing. A clip path or a mask removes all three. Two steps of a scale are a pixel apart, or they are one step. A scale offers a choice, and a choice no screen can draw is not one. Steps derived from a shape by a ratio collapse when the shape is fine: half and three quarters of a 3 px radius are 0.75 px apart. A system that derives its steps measures them on the contours they are meant for, and falls back to steps that can be told apart.
